Due November 22, 2024
Goal: Raise the public alarm bells about information manipulation, particularly how foreign
malign influence campaigns from strategic competitors are being used to spread false
information about USAID's programming, staff, and purpose. Provide some of the most eye-
popping examples and stats describing the problem and the solutions we've piloted/are
proposing on how to better address it. Also explain how Al is impacting each of the below
categories.
Examples & data points of FMI campaigns targeting USAID:
Foreign and non-state actors in the countries in which USAID operates overseas are using
emerging and existing technologies to manipulate and control information at a higher speed and
scale than ever before. Information manipulation by foreign state and non-state actors abroad
can have significant and enduring impacts on development and can create direct operational
and reputational risk to USAID, including its staff, programs, and implementing partners,
especially those working in local contexts. This problem affects USAID across all contexts and
all technical sectors-from democracy to critical infrastructure, economic growth and innovation,
education, global health, stability, and food security—and can prevent the Agency from
achieving its development objectives.
Below are further examples of foreign malign information manipulation campaigns targeting
USAID programs, people, and partners.
Global
"The Hypocrisy and Facts of United States Foreign Aid," the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the
People's Republic of China (April 19, 2024).
The story: On April 19, 2024, the People's Republic of China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA)
released a publication titled "The Hypocrisy and Facts of the United States Foreign Aid,"
targeting USAID. The primary aim of this article is to undermine the credibility of U.S. foreign
assistance efforts while promoting PRC's aid initiatives as altruistic and beneficial. The MFA has
since posted this article on dozens of social media and messaging accounts globally.
→ Content examples: Chinese Embassy in Zimbabwe on Twitter; op-ed in the Global Times
The impact: Information Manipulation such as the article will corrode trust in USAID in our
partner countries and limit USAID's ability to execute its Mission. Based on recent examples of
Russian information operations in West Africa, similar reputational assaults have caused some
host country governments to pause or slow down cooperation (e.g. Nigeria following the rumors
about USG public health programs). These assaults damage the effectiveness of our foreign
assistance programs, and can create doubt and reluctance with intended beneficiaries of that
assistance.

Africa
In Africa, Russia has conducted years of aggressive information manipulation efforts to
accelerate "anti-colonial" "self-determination" narratives and disaffection with France, and
Russian state-backed messengers have sought to lump the United States with that.
Reputational attacks on our assistance this year have most visibly been on our USG public
health work, whipping up false conspiracy narratives, some old tropes about HIV-AIDS, but also
newer ones on malaria and dengue fever, etc. African government reactions have been uneven,
with some fairly consistent partners such as Nigeria having paused advancing some work with
USAID, and troublesome state agencies like Burkina Faso's Ministry of Health having gone
public defending the USG. USAID is often referenced in false narratives alongside DTRA
(falsely accused of bio weapons labs globally) and CDC, and we have created a good working
relationship with DTRA and their new Office of Information Resilience.
"Russian Intelligence Is Pushing False Claims of U.S. Biological Testing in Africa, U.S. Says,"
The Wall Street Journal (February 8, 2024).
The story: Russian state-backed messengers spread false information about USAID's health
work on the African continent. "Russian intelligence agencies are trying to undermine U.S.
influence in Africa by spreading disinformation that Africans have been the unwitting test
subjects in Pentagon biological research programs and casting aspersions on Western public-
health programs, U.S. officials said."
The response: The GEC went public with its efforts to disrupt this campaign with an article in
The Wall Street Journal.
"Russia's Latest Target in Africa: U.S.-Funded Anti-Malaria Programs," The New York Times
(October 14, 2024).
The story: "The scientists sifting through thousands of genetically modified mosquito larvae in
a laboratory in Burkina Faso were trying to stop the spread of malaria, one of the
biggest killers on the African continent. But in the pro-Russian propaganda telling of their work,
the scientists, helped by funding from the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, were not protecting
local people against malaria, they were infecting them."
The impact: African government reactions have been uneven, with some fairly consistent
partners such as Nigeria pausing some work with USAID, and traditionally troublesome states
like Burkina Faso's Ministry of Health publicly defending the U.S. government.
"Putin's Media Blitz on Africa Food Crisis Sparks Alarm in Europe," Bloomberg (July 3, 2022);
"Russia's Disinformation Cannot Hide its Responsibility for the Global Food Crisis," GEC (June
22, 2022).
The story: "Food insecurity has risen because of Putin's war of choice. It was not caused, as
the Kremlin claims, by sanctions that the United States and many other countries have imposed
in response to Russia's horrific aggression against Ukraine."
→ Content examples: Russian Embassy in Kenya on Twitter; Sputnik Turkiye
(SBU) The response: Please see here. As a result, Vera and LPA launched a proactive food
security campaign to address this info manipulation.

Asia
"Is US Plotting Electoral Coup in Solomon Islands?" Sputnik (April 9, 2024).
The story: Russian state-backed outlet Sputnik published an "investigation" into USAID's
alleged role in "an electoral coup" in the Solomon Islands. Sputnik claimed that it had received a
trove of documents from a source with supposed "intimate knowledge" of USAID's activities in
the region; however, USAID was able to confirm that several - if not all - of these documents
were forged. Following the Sputnik publication, the PRC state-backed outlet Global Times
published its own "investigation" on alleged U.S. interference, claiming that "the US and its allies
appear to be using 'color revolution' tactics to infiltrate the political landscape of the Solomon
Islands." These claims were also amplified by the Solomon Islands' government, and the
narrative was picked up by Indonesian media. Following the U.S. Embassy's response, Sputnik
and the Global Times, as well as other PRC state-backed actors, doubled down on their claims.
The impact: The impact this narrative had on the results of the election or the perception of
USAID is unclear; however, it is noteworthy that this follows up on a 2021 PRC information
manipulation campaign against the U.S. government in Solomon Islands that aimed to oust the
pro-U.S. premier of Malaita province and generate distrust of the U.S. government and U.S.
foreign assistance. Related to this episode, another media partner who was working with us on
a strategic communications campaign in the Solomon Islands backed out of the project. It was
discovered that they were also working with the PRC.
The response: The U.S. Embassy to Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands, and Vanuatu
released a public statement refuting the false claims. (SBU) Please also see here.
Europe and Eurasia
"Public Health Fakes: USAID supplies drugs to the Ukrainian military," VoxUkraine (September
8, 2023).
The story: "At the end of July and the beginning of August, an information attack against the
Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) and the United States Agency for International Development
(USAID) started simultaneously on several platforms (Facebook, Twitter, Telegram, and
YouTube). The authors of fake posts claimed that in a published video, soldiers of the 79th
Separate Airborne Assault Brigade of the AFU in Zaporizhzhia were receiving ephedrine from
USAID. Some channels refer to ephedrine as a stimulant necessary for producing
methamphetamine, while others directly label this substance as a drug. The new video is being
attempted to be linked to the old narrative of Russian propaganda about 'combat drugs of the
AFU,' which allegedly alleviate pain and boost the combat morale of Ukrainians."
→ Content example: Russian Embassy in Bulgaria on Telegram
"Georgia demands US explain funding potential revolution in country," TASS Russian News
Agency (October 2, 2023).
The story: In October 2023, the ruling Georgian Dream party falsely accused USAID of plotting
a color revolution in the country. Russian state-backed media picked up the story, with TASS

reporting that members of the Georgian Dream party were calling on USAID to "provide
clarification on the issue of USAID funding trainings in Georgia that involved Serbian citizens
preparing the republic's residents to overthrow the authorities of the country."
The impact: While it cannot be directly traced to a single instance of information manipulation,
in May 2024, Georgian Parliament passed a "foreign influence" law, which has made it more
difficult for USAID to operate in support of shared development objectives in the country.
The response: On October 26, 2023, in an interview with Civil Georgia, Ambassador Erin
Elizabeth McKee, USAID Assistant Administrator for Europe and Eurasia, refuted allegations by
the ruling Georgian Dream party that USAID is "funding extremists" in Georgia through
Georgian NGO projects.
Latin America and the Caribbean
Colombia
The story: A defamatory video created and circulated by local actors in Colombia accused
USAID and local implementing partners of trying to take over the government and influence
political processes.
The impact: The video's creators aimed to diminish trust of the United States and our partners.
USAID staff and implementing partners were put at risk.
The response: USAID decided not to respond to this instance of information manipulation with
a campaign. Because the spread of the video was limited to a relatively small number of people
whose online activity remained isolated from the wider public, creating content to counter the
narrative may have inadvertently led to the narrative gaining more traction than it otherwise
would have.
Middle East
"Intentions," Iran's Press TV (September 13, 2023).
The story: In September 2023, Iranian state-backed outlet Press TV produced a documentary-
style video arguing that "American organizations such as USAID, USIP, and NED have reached
out to the people of the Middle East, trying to maintain their hegemony in the region through
their seemingly cultural, humanitarian projects."

(U) FIVE CASE EXAMPLES - Security Threats and Exploitation Risks Linked to
Information Manipulation Targeting USAID
(U) The analysis of excerpts from five previously reported cases highlight examples of security
threats and vulnerabilities tied to suspected Foreign Malign Influence (FMI) that target USAID.

These cases demonstrate how adverse actors might exploit social media and geopolitical
sensitivities to potentially undermine USAID's reputation, operational integrity, and personnel
safety.
(U) CASE EXAMPLE # 1 - Central African Republic: NGO Exploitation Risks
Analytic Notes: The following report underscores vulnerabilities in NGO operations in conflict-
prone regions. The Central African Republic (CAR) has seen NGOs, including USAID-funded
entities, operate under conditions where state authority is weak and foreign actors exert
significant influence. This environment is ripe for FMI exploitation by adverse actors, as NGOs
may be falsely associated with foreign agendas or become targets for information
manipulation. The situation reflects how false narratives could undermine trust in USAID's
humanitarian initiatives, potentially reducing local cooperation and increasing operational risks.
Details: Analysts identified concerning reports of manipulated information mentioning the
United States Agency for International Development (USAID) in the Central African Republic
(CAR), in relation to a recent detainment. The detainment of a consultant affiliated with the
U.S. NGO FHI360 has sparked a cascade of false narratives, pointing fingers at the U.S.
government and USAID, accusing both of nefarious activities. According to the USAID Africa
Bureau, the detained individual is not a U.S. citizen and was not working on a USAID project.
However, pro-Russian propaganda outlets and various social media platforms have
disseminated information, linking the individual to USAID and alleging espionage activities
intended to destabilize CAR. The spread of these narratives poses a risk to the organization's
reputation and operational stability in CAR and potentially other regions in Africa. Classified
reporting available with additional details.
Key Findings: The narrative began with a slew of articles from well-known pro-Russian
propaganda sites such as Ndjoni Sango, Lengo Songo, and Afrique Media. These sources allege
that the individual, a consultant with FHI360 on behalf of USAID, was not only recruiting Fulani
individuals to form a terrorist group akin to ISIS but also attempting to bribe members of the
Azande Ani Kpigbi militia to cooperate with the U.S. government. This baseless claim has been
spreading rapidly, sowing seeds of distrust and fear among the local populace.
An important highlight from this narrative is the conflicting reports surrounding the individual's
identity. Some sources describe him as an American, while others label him as an American
NGO employee associated with USAID. This lack of clarity and inconsistency is a clear indicator
of deliberate information manipulation, designed to create confusion and falsely implicate the
U.S. in destabilizing CAR.

(U) A closer look at the sentiment behind these narratives reveals a predominantly negative
tone. Most of the content is disseminated in English, with French being the second most
common language. This linguistic choice suggests a targeted effort to reach both US and
Francophone African audiences, amplifying the negative impact of the false narratives in the
region.
The reach of these false narratives extends beyond CAR. In a notable instance, the Ghanaian
online news outlet PEACEFMONLINE.COM has also propagated the accusation that USAID was
attempting to infiltrate CAR's judicial system. At this time, analysts are not clear on whether
this news outlet is affiliated with any other foreign government or has a history of pushing
foreign malign information. However, this regional spread indicates a broader strategy to
undermine USAID's reputation across Africa, highlighting the pervasive nature of this
information campaign.
Despite the widespread dissemination of these damaging narratives, the assessment did not
identify immediate threats to USAID personnel or programs in CAR. The primary objective of
these false claims appears to focus on undermining USAID's reputation and credibility rather
than inciting direct harm to its staff. Nevertheless, the potential for reputational damage and
operational disruptions cannot be underestimated. As such, analysts will continue to monitor
online narratives and activity for negative mentions of USAID in relation to CAR.
This incident sheds light on the sophisticated and multi-faceted nature of foreign malign
influence campaigns targeting USAID in CAR. The deliberate spread of ambiguous information,
conflicting reports, and negative sentiment pose significant challenges to USAID's mission and
operations.
SOURCING: Sourcing information for this report is derived from advanced data and analytics
provided by Babel Street, a global information intelligence platform utilized to monitor trends,
identify patterns, and enhance decision-making in identity, threat, and risk mitigation
operations. Additionally, insights were supplemented by field reports, contributions from
employed field personnel, and reporting from a humanitarian association that supports aid
agencies, healthcare providers, educators, protection services, and other civil society
organizations by delivering publicly available information to inform evidence-based policies.
(U) CASE EXAMPLE # 2 - Zimbabwe: Hostile Narratives Against USAID
(U) Analytic Notes: The summary report on Zimbabwe reveals a multi-faceted disinformation
campaign targeting USAID. Narratives around a fatal car accident, alleged espionage, nepotism,

and calls for expelling USAID from Zimbabwe demonstrate how isolated incidents can be
weaponized to erode USAID's credibility. The accusation of regime change support aligns with
broader FMI strategies to portray USAID as an agent of Western interference. These narratives,
if amplified, could jeopardize USAID's projects by diminishing local trust, increasing resistance,
and potentially endangering personnel.
(U) Details: Prior to a visit of the USAID Africa Bureau to Zimbabwe, SEC identified four
concerning narratives on social media and online content that have the potential to adversely
affect the perception of USAID in the region. These narratives highlight potential risks to
USAID's reputation and the effectiveness of its ongoing and future projects in Zimbabwe. The
identified issues range from a fatal car accident involving a USAID-affiliated vehicle to broader
accusations of espionage, nepotism, and calls for the expulsion of USAID from the country.
These findings suggest a growing mistrust and hostility towards USAID's presence and activities
in Zimbabwe.
(U) Key Findings:
1. (U) USAID-Related Fatal Road Accident in Chipinge
A news article titled "USAID car accident kills a Zimbabwean in Chipinge" on the local
news website Bulawayo24 reported a fatal road accident involving a vehicle associated
with a USAID-funded project. The Zimbabwean driver, an employee of an implementing
partner organization, was involved in the incident. The project team is cooperating with
police and local officials. This incident has the potential to generate negative sentiments
towards USAID, particularly if it is perceived as a result of negligence or poor oversight.
2. (U) Allegations of USAID Supporting Regime Change
Online sentiments expressed by some locals suggest that USAID's projects are perceived
as being focused on regime change in Zimbabwe. These claims have been exacerbated
by recent allegations that a USAID-supported spy ring was busted and deported from
Zimbabwe. This narrative feeds into a broader distrust of USAID's intentions in the
country and could lead to increased resistance to USAID initiatives.
3. (U) Accusations of Nepotism
Analysts identified anti-USAID sentiments on social media accusing the organization of
supporting nepotism in Zimbabwe. While no specific evidence or context was provided,
this allegation contributes to a broader narrative that USAID is covertly interfering in

Zimbabwe's government. Such accusations, even when unfounded, can undermine the
legitimacy of USAID's work and erode trust among the local population.
4. (U) Call for Action Against USAID
A call for action was found on social media urging the cessation of all USAID activities in
Zimbabwe, the closure of the US Embassy in Harare, and the expulsion of all USAID
personnel from the country. The post also called for Zimbabweans in the US to return
home. This post reflects an extreme anti-USAID sentiment and suggests a potential risk
of escalation in public opposition to USAID's presence in Zimbabwe.
Impact Assessment: The identified narratives present a risk to USAID's operations and
reputation in Zimbabwe. The fatal road accident, while seemingly an isolated incident, could be
used to fuel negative perceptions of USAID as negligent or careless. Allegations of espionage,
regime change, and nepotism contribute to an image of USAID as an external force attempting
to interfere in Zimbabwean affairs, which can undermine local support for USAID projects. The
call for action to expel USAID from Zimbabwe is particularly concerning, as it suggests a
potential mobilization of public sentiment against the organization. If these narratives gain
traction, they could lead to increased resistance to USAID initiatives, decreased cooperation
from local partners, and potential safety risks for USAID personnel on the ground.
SOURCING: Sourcing information for this report is derived from advanced data and analytics
provided by Babel Street, a global information intelligence platform utilized to monitor
trends, identify patterns, and enhance decision-making in identity, threat, and risk mitigation
operations.
(U) CASE EXAMPLE # 3 - Venezuela: Coup Allegations and Russian Amplification
(U) Analytic Notes: The report on Venezuela details of what appears to be an organized
information manipulation campaign accusing USAID of orchestrating a coup during
controversial presidential elections. Russian and Venezuelan state media, along with
coordinated social media troll accounts, amplify these false narratives to frame USAID as a
destabilizing force. This case highlights the intersection of geopolitical rivalry and FMI tactics,
where USAID becomes a target in broader anti-Western propaganda efforts. The allegations not
only risk USAID's reputation but also foster hostility in a politically volatile region.
Details: Analysts identified online narratives accusing USAID of supporting a coup in Venezuela,
coinciding with the controversial presidential elections. These claims, likely driven by a foreign
influence operations, allege USAID's involvement in destabilization efforts. The narratives are

being amplified by Russian and Venezuelan state media, as well as possible coordinated troll
accounts on social media.
Key Findings: In the past three weeks, there has been a significant increase in online content
accusing USAID and other Western NGOs of supporting a coup in Venezuela. This surge in
hostile messaging appears closely tied to the recent Venezuelan presidential elections, where
both President Nicolás Maduro and opposition candidate Edmundo González claimed victory.
Despite exit polls indicating an opposition win, Venezuela's electoral authority announced
Maduro's re-election with 51% of the vote, leading to widespread controversy and international
criticism, particularly from Western nations and the Biden Administration, regarding the
fairness of the electoral process.
The possible uptick in anti-US rhetoric targeting USAID coincides with this international
backlash and appears to be part of a broader narrative, suggesting that USAID collaborated in
orchestrating a large-scale operation involving terrorism, cyberattacks, and psychological
warfare to destabilize Venezuela. Notably, this narrative aligns with known Russian influence
tactics, as Russia considers Venezuela a key ally in Latin America. Russian state media,
especially RT in Spanish, and Venezuelan state-run channels like Venezolana de Televisión
(VTV), have increasingly amplified false narratives, portraying the United States as an
imperialist aggressor while casting Russia as a defender of the oppressed.
Analysts have identified several instances of claims mentioning USAID coup involvement in
Venezuela spreading across social media platforms, including Facebook and Twitter, as well as
on public media channels like SouthFront, a site linked to Russian influence operations. One
particular piece of content, linked to SouthFront, claimed that opposition forces set fire to a
USAID truck on the Venezuelan border. Analysts are currently vetting this claim and will provide
an update on the findings. However, the social media profiles propagating these messages
display characteristics typical of troll accounts, such as anonymous identities, high levels of
activity, repetitive posting, and coordination in spreading similar narratives.
SOURCING: Sourcing information for this report is derived from advanced data and analytics
provided by Babel Street, a global information intelligence platform utilized to monitor trends,
identify patterns, and enhance decision-making in identity, threat, and risk mitigation
operations.
(U) CASE EXAMPLE # 4 - Kyrgyzstan: USAID Staff Targeted via Social Media

Analytic Notes: The analysis of the Telegram channel "Ачуу чындык" demonstrates how FMI
actors exploit social media platforms to spread disinformation targeting USAID personnel, such
as Mission Director Sara Werth. Allegations of CIA connections and military affiliations, despite
lacking evidence, aim to delegitimize USAID's humanitarian efforts. While there are no
immediate threats, the high engagement rate of the channel suggests a risk of narrative
escalation. This example illustrates how misinformation can isolate USAID representatives and
hinder their ability to build trust with local stakeholders.
Details: This report analyzes the content and impact of a Telegram channel named "Ачуу
чындык" (translated as "Bitter Truth"), which recently published posts concerning Sara Werth,
the USAID Mission Director for Kyrgyzstan. The channel, which poses as a media outlet but
resembles an independent blog, has shared allegations about Ms. Werth's professional
background, claiming that she is connected to the CIA and has a military role, contrary to her
publicly listed experience with the Peace Corps.
(U) Key Findings: The "Ачуу чындык" Telegram channel is relatively active, with 2.1k followers,
176 average post views, and an engagement rate of 5%, which is higher than the typical 2%-3%
seen on social media. The channel predominantly uses Kyrgyz and Russian, and has amassed
6,135 total posts. This indicates a sustained presence with a high level of interaction, making it
an influential platform for shaping narratives within certain circles.
The posts in question allege that the USAID Mission Director's (Sara Werth)background includes
military service and connections to the CIA, rather than solely humanitarian work. The posts
reference the National Defense University's website to support claims that she holds the rank
of a military colonel with the goal of shaping foreign policy. Additionally, the channel suggests
that her work in Kyrgyzstan is focused on promoting democracy under the guise of economic
and humanitarian projects.
(U) Further investigation identified a YouTube channel affiliated with "Ачуу чындык," with
1.71k subscribers, 359 videos, and 170,955 views. The channel's registered location is Poland,
and it was established on March 8, 2022. The existence of multiple platforms suggests a
coordinated effort to amplify the messaging, though no direct analysis of the channel's content
was conducted. A TikTok account was also found, but its contents remain unanalyzed.
Independent searches of Kyrgyz and Russian media outlets yielded 42 sites mentioning Sara
Werth, none of which appeared nefarious or suggestive of harmful intent. This indicates that
while the Telegram posts may attempt to shape perceptions, they have not been widely echoed
in mainstream media. At this time, there are no direct threats or signs of targeting towards Sara
Werth or the USAID Mission in Kyrgyzstan. Although the posts contain information that may not

be factually accurate, there is no immediate evidence of threats of harm or incitement related
to these claims.
The "Ачуу чындык" channel is actively disseminating unverified claims about Sara Werth,
casting doubt on her humanitarian credentials and suggesting covert military affiliations.
However, despite the questionable accuracy of these claims, there is no indication that these
posts are part of a larger coordinated campaign to harm Ms. Werth or her mission. The
channel's reach, coupled with its high engagement rate, does warrant continued monitoring to
assess whether these narratives gain further traction or escalate into more serious threats.
SOURCING: Sourcing information for this report is derived from advanced data and analytics
provided by Babel Street, a global information intelligence platform utilized to monitor trends,
identify patterns, and enhance decision-making in identity, threat, and risk mitigation
operations. Additionally, insights were supplemented by field reports and contributions from
employed personnel.
(U) CASE EXAMPLE # 5 - Information Manipulation Campaign Targeting USAID
Personnel
(U) Analytic Notes: The findings on USAID personnel being targeted in Yemen highlight how
false narratives not only erode trust but also pose significant security risks (i.e. being accused of
espionage in a foreign country can result in harassment, detention, or severe penalties like
imprisonment). This jeopardizes the safety of USAID personnel, making them targets of local
hostility and legal action, and threatens the viability of their humanitarian work.
Details: This report details the ongoing information manipulation campaign aimed at
discrediting USAID and its personnel by spreading narratives that accuse the organization of
espionage activities. This specific campaign alleges USAID embeds spies within its operations,
undermining its humanitarian missions. The report identifies the scope and impact of these
disinformation narratives, particularly focusing on a list of named individuals and analyzing their
digital footprint and exposure.
The campaign against USAID has primarily spread through social media platforms, online
discussion forums, and various news websites, both national and foreign. At this time it does
not appear as if there is virality to the ongoing claims due to limited engagement on social
media posts. The narrative asserts that USAID is a front for espionage operations, with specific
personnel allegedly acting as spies. Despite thorough investigation, no personal information or
evidence has been found to substantiate these claims against the listed individuals.

The individuals named have minimal digital footprints, with no personal information available
to put them at significant risk. The campaign's persistence and the involvement of various
media outlets highlight the need for continuous monitoring and proactive communication
strategies to protect USAID's reputation.
The following names are USAID personnel whose names have been reported for being
mentioned in the false narratives:
1. Sofia Quesada
2. Cybill Sigler
3. Christopher Jennings
4. Julie Pekowski
5. Jennifer Link
6. Elizabeth Feary
7. Todd Sorenson
8. Brittany Gleixner-Hayat
9. Julie Koenen
10. Mei Mei Peng
11. Oddo Oghale
12. Andrew Plitt
Digital Footprint Analysis: SEC conducted searches across more than 15 social media platforms,
various discussion forums, and dark web sources. The results are as follows:
• Social Media Platforms: No significant or sensitive personal information was found
related to the listed individuals. Their digital footprints are minimal, and no posts or
profiles suggest involvement in espionage activities.
• Discussion Forums: Searches yielded zero results; there were no mentions or
discussions involving the listed individuals.
• Dark Web: Analysts conducted several searches using variations of the individuals'
names and found nothing significant that could pose a risk or threaten them.
Media Outlets Spreading False Messaging: SEC identified that the campaign against USAID has
been amplified by both foreign and national news sites, with several articles contributing to the
spread of the false narrative. The following media outlets were identified:
Foreign News Sites:
• PressTV (Iran)
• The Times of Israel

• Middle East Monitor
• Saba Yemen
• Ava Press (Afghan Voice Agency)
•Islamic Republic News Agency
ABNA News Agency
• Yemen Press Agency
National News Sites:
• The Washington Post
• ABC News
Analysis of IM Spread: According to analysts findings, the disinformation campaign's primary
tactic appears to sow doubt about USAID's humanitarian work by labeling its employees as
spies, continuing an aged narrative that USAID works alongside spy agencies. This narrative
continues to gain traction primarily through foreign news outlets, with rare moments of
national sites amplifying the stories. The intention appears to be to undermine USAID's
credibility in the region and disrupt its operations by causing mistrust among the populations it
serves.
UPDATES OF 22 AUG 24: The report on information manipulation targeting USAID personnel
has evolved since its last update in June 2024. New findings indicate that the information
manipulation campaign, which accuses USAID of embedding spies within its operations, has
continued efforts to expand/maintain its reach, especially within the Middle East and North
Africa (MENA) region. The campaign has been fueled by an increased number of local news
broadcasts and articles from regional news outlets, particularly in Yemen, which continue to
amplify the false narrative.
Recent analyses highlight that the false information spread has become more coordinated,
leveraging both traditional media and social media platforms. The content has become more
tailored to specific regional audiences to increase distrust in USAID's humanitarian efforts.
Despite these developments, the digital footprints of the named USAID personnel in the initial
report remain minimal, with no new personal information being exposed that could increase
their risk. However, new personnel information is noted for this update.
Key Findings: Analysts identified an additional article on Al Masirah titled, Foreign Intelligence
Networks Undermining Yemen's Sovereignty: The Role of USAID's RGP Project and NDI. This
article is an example of a targeted campaign against USAID by accusing it of being involved in a
broader foreign intelligence operation aimed at destabilizing Yemen. The article makes several
claims to undermine the credibility and legitimacy of USAID's initiatives in Yemen, particularly

the "RGP Project," by portraying it as a tool for espionage and subversion rather than a genuine
development effort.
Additionally, the article claims that the "RGP Project" exacerbated social and political tensions,
fueled corruption, and contributed to regional instability. It asserts that the project was
mismanaged and exploited for illicit purposes, further casting doubt on USAID's role in Yemen.
It should also be noted that the article declared a link to USAID and a supposed spy network
associated with the CIA and Israeli Mossad, the article suggests that USAID's activities in
Yemen were part of a larger intelligence operation which supports the claims mentioned in
the initial report.
Additional Individuals Targeted: Separate from the identified article, the ME Mission has
reported that additional USAID staff have been implicated as alleged members of the spy ring.
Analysts have conducted comprehensive social media searches in both English and Arabic for
these individuals and variations of their names to identify any additional targeted messaging or
narratives surrounding them.
The following names are additional USAID personnel whose names have been reported for
being mentioned in the false narratives:
1. Allison Minor
2. Herbert (Herbie) Smith
3. Tammy Hermez Sanchez (no record)
Digital Footprint Analysis: SEC conducted thorough searches across over 15 social media
platforms, various discussion forums, and dark web sources. The findings are as follows:
• Social Media Platforms: No significant or sensitive personal information related to the
listed individuals was discovered. Their digital footprints are minimal, with no posts or
profiles personating them or claims of any involvement in espionage activities.
• Discussion Forums: The searches yielded no results; there were no mentions or
discussions involving the listed individuals.
• Dark Web: Multiple searches using variations of the individuals' names revealed no
significant information that could pose a risk or threat to them.
SOURCING: Sourcing information for this report is derived from advanced data and analytics
provided by Babel Street, a global information intelligence platform utilized to monitor trends,
identify patterns, and enhance decision-making in identity, threat, and risk mitigation

operations. Additionally, insights were supplemented by field reports and contributions from

(U) ADDITIONAL POTENTIAL SECURITY AND SAFETY RISK CASE SUMMARIES
(U) Increased Hostility Towards Personnel
• Additional Reporting:
• Humanitarian Aid Discourse In Burkina Faso
• Social Media Monitoring and Aid in the Context of the Libyan Flooding
Disaster
• Viral Allegations Against IP in Burkina Faso
• Risks: The reports highlight findings of hostility towards humanitarian personnel driven
by information manipulation and the online amplification of negative narratives. In
Burkina Faso, social media discussions about aid organizations, including USAID,
revealed predominantly positive sentiment but also notable negative reactions. These
were often triggered by edited media and manipulative information campaigns, with
accusations ranging from espionage to insufficient investment. Most hostility emerged
in comment sections, reflecting either possible genuine opinions or targeted
information manipulation strategies. At this time, analysts are unable to determine
which one. Similarly, in the aftermath of Storm Daniel in Libya, anti-USAID sentiment
surged online, particularly on Facebook, where groups promoting opposition to USAID
activities were identified. Despite no immediate threats of violence, these narratives
raise safety risks for USAID/BHA staff, necessitating ongoing monitoring.
In another instance, a possible implementing partner, the Burkinabè Red Cross faced
viral allegations of complicity in jihadist attacks following false claims that it had prior
knowledge of an assault and withdrew staff from the area. These allegations, spread
through WhatsApp and Facebook, significantly undermined trust in humanitarian
organizations. Although the Red Cross publicly denied the claims, the widespread belief
in these accusations eroded public confidence, complicating aid delivery and local
cooperation.
Across all cases, information manipulation campaigns weaponize social media to
damage the credibility of humanitarian organizations and foster distrust. The
amplification of false narratives on online platforms creates an environment of hostility,

exposing personnel to psychological stress, reputational harm, and potential physical
threats.
(U) Narratives Linking USAID to Espionage
• Additional Reporting:
• Russian Claims Against USAID Implementing Partners
• Unveiling Foreign Malign Influence Narratives: Targeting FHI 360-USAID in the
Central African Republic
• Summary Report: Zimbabwe Anti-USAID Narratives
• Venezuela: Claims of USAID Supporting a Coup
• Risks: The reports collectively demonstrate how allegations of espionage and covert
influence operations against USAID and its implementing partners heighten risks to
personnel and operations. In Zimbabwe, narratives accusing USAID of supporting regime
change and operating a spy network have fueled calls for the expulsion of USAID and its
staff from the country. These claims, though unsubstantiated, contribute to growing
mistrust and hostility, increasing the potential for personnel to face legal action or
violence if these narratives gain further traction. Similarly, in the Central African
Republic, a consultant affiliated with FHI360 became the subject of false accusations of
espionage, with manipulated narratives suggesting U.S. involvement in destabilizing the
region. This case underscores how pro-Russian propaganda and ambiguous reporting
amplify hostility, posing reputational and operational risks.
In Venezuela, claims alleging USAID's involvement in a coup have been amplified by
state media and coordinated online campaigns. Narratives accuse USAID of
orchestrating terrorism, cyberattacks, and psychological warfare, painting the
organization as a tool of imperialist aggression. This rhetoric not only erodes trust in
USAID's humanitarian mission but also places staff at risk of retaliation, legal
repercussions, or targeted violence.
In Russia, accusations that USAID initiatives, such as the educational All Children
Succeeding Activity in Uzbekistan, serve as fronts for recruiting "agents of influence"
highlight how malign information manipulation aims to discredit legitimate aid efforts.
While no evidence supports these claims, they align with a broader strategy to
undermine Western NGOs and create an environment of suspicion and hostility. The
underlying theme in all cases is the use of information manipulation to portray
humanitarian projects as fronts for espionage or covert influence. Such allegations
increase the risk of staff being detained, harassed, or subjected to violence, especially in

regions where governments or local populations are predisposed to distrust foreign aid
organizations.
(U) ADDITIONAL POTENTIAL REPUTATIONAL AND BRANDING RISK CASE
SUMMARIES
(U) False Allegations of Political Interference
• Additional Reporting:
• Examining China Daily News Accusations against USAID and CNN News
• Analytical Report on PRC Messaging Concerning USAID's Humanitarian Efforts in
Sudan
• Risks: The reports highlight how accusations of political interference could threaten
USAID's reputation and brand, particularly in regions with strong foreign influence
operations. In Sudan, PRC-backed media narratives portray USAID's humanitarian
initiatives as politically motivated, framing them as an infringement on Sudanese
sovereignty. This messaging, aligned with Sudan's rhetoric of self-reliance, casts USAID
as a foreign actor undermining local governance. Such narratives erode trust among
local communities and governments, fostering resentment and opposition to USAID's
projects. This reputational risk is compounded by the potential for stricter regulations,
reduced access for personnel, and challenges in securing partnerships, limiting USAID's
operational effectiveness in the region
Similarly, China Daily's accusations against USAID allege that it funds disinformation
campaigns to suppress Chinese media outlets, such as its TikTok account, Media
Unlocked. These claims, though baseless, are part of a broader strategy to discredit
USAID by portraying it as a manipulative entity pursuing political aims. While these
narratives currently have limited engagement, they reach significant audiences,
amplifying the potential for long-term reputational harm. Such efforts distract from
USAID's humanitarian objectives and create skepticism about its intentions, making it
more challenging to maintain credibility and trust globally
Collectively, these narratives reflect a pattern of information manipulation that seeks to
undermine USAID's integrity by casting its efforts as politically driven rather than
altruistic. This poses risks to the agency's brand, complicates its ability to deliver aid,
and potentially disrupts its relationships with host nations.

(U) Claims of Aid Mismanagement and Corruption
• Additional Reporting:
• Analysis of Foreign Malign Influence and Information Manipulation in Georgia
• Report on Sputnik Article "USAID Failing to Monitor Ukraine Aid Programs
Thoroughly"
• Risks: The reports underscore how allegations of aid mismanagement and corruption
pose reputational and branding risks to USAID, particularly in politically and socially
sensitive contexts. In Ukraine, a Sputnik article criticized USAID's oversight of aid
programs, claiming a failure to monitor the effective use of funds. This narrative
selectively highlighted perceived inefficiencies without offering a balanced perspective,
fostering a skewed perception among readers. Disseminated across multiple platforms,
including VK and Facebook, the narrative gained traction, inciting negative sentiment.
Similarly, in Georgia, anti-USAID rhetoric emerged amidst the controversial
Transparency of Foreign Influence law. Narratives accused USAID of funding protests
through IREX, framing the agency as interfering in local politics. These allegations tap
into broader suspicions that USAID serves as a front for covert operations, compounding
local mistrust. Although these claims have not yet gained significant traction, they align
with a long-standing narrative of USAID misusing funds for political manipulation, which
could undermine its credibility and partnership potential in the region.
These claims of mismanagement and corruption not only tarnish USAID's reputation but
also risk diminishing local and international support for its initiatives. Such narratives
can foster resistance from host governments, skepticism among aid recipients, and
reluctance from stakeholders to collaborate, ultimately hindering USAID's ability to
fulfill its mission effectively.
Coordination with the Private Sector:
We recognize that information manipulation and foreign malign influence have spread on social
media, and Al is amplifying the speed and scale of this online threat. Below are a few examples

of how foreign malign actors have used Al to manipulate information - sometimes going
against Al companies' own policies.
• Ahead of Moldova's October 2024 election, Russian state-backed actors produced
deepfake videos of President Maia Sandu in an attempt to undercut her support.
• Pro-PRC, Al-generated "news anchors" attempted to sway the Taiwanese presidential
election in May 2024.
• In the lead-up to the Indonesian election in February 2024, now-President Prabowo
Subianto, the former Defense Minister who is accused of abusing human rights during
the Suharto era, successfully rebranded himself as a "cuddly grandpa" using generative
Al.
While we do not have explicit evidence or metrics about how Al has been used to target
USAID's programs, people, or partners, given the growing prevalence of Al, we suspect that it is
being exploited to spread information manipulation on social media channels targeting USAID.
We also acknowledge the essential role that technology companies play in addressing the
threat of information manipulation. USAID has partnered with technology companies to
strengthen development outcomes and address foreign malign information manipulation through
several initiatives:
• The Advancing Digital Democracy (ADD) Academy builds upon the ADD initiative
announced at the first Summit for Democracy. In partnership with multinational
technology companies, ADD Academy will offer essential skills training in cybersecurity,
data privacy, cloud computing, and responsible Al, among other topics. In the initial
phase, ADD Academy intends to work with anchor technology partners Cloudflare,
Google, and Microsoft.
• In Indonesia, USAID partnered with a local technology company to create Gali Fakta, an
award-winning game that teaches players online literacy skills.
Opportunities for Future Policy Interventions:
To meet the challenges posed by foreign malign information manipulation, USAID must
increase its investments in affirmative strategic communications. USAID's impact in partner
countries is not going to be as effective as it can be unless we can show citizens the impact of
our work. It is essential that we meet people where they are and tell our story in a way that
speaks to them. To do so, we need to better understand where our audience gets their news in
each country, and we need to equip DOCs with the tools and skills to reach these audiences
and to show the benefits that USAID is delivering.
Beyond equipping DOCs, we need to equip the entire USAID workforce and our partners with a
greater understanding of media literacy, digital literacy, and Al, so they are prepared both to
recognize information manipulation and to respond to it through strategic communications and
effective programming - especially when they themselves are targeted.

Furthermore, USAID, and the U.S. government more broadly, needs to hold threat actors
accountable. We should continue to push for greater interagency coordination on foreign malign
influence. When appropriate and when it advances the United States' national security
objectives, we should push to expose foreign information manipulation and declassify
intelligence in order to put foreign malign state actors on notice.
Investing in the media and technology spaces in partner countries is also essential. Foreign
malign actors including the PRC are investing in media and technology companies in
developing countries around the world — including in Zambia, Peru, and Nigeria — which puts
freedom of speech, citizens' data, and U.S. national security at risk. The PRC is signing MOUs
with many of our development partners and is investing in technology infrastructure to give
citizens access to technology as a way to control and surveil citizens. When the PRC and other
foreign malign actors control the technology and media space, they are equally capable of
spreading manipulated content against USAID staff, partners, and programs. This is why
investing in initiatives like the Advancing Digital Democracy Initiative is critical to countering the
PRC and other foreign malign adversaries.
USAID's competitive advantage is our development model. The Agency is improving outcomes
for people around the world across all sectors, ranging from energy to governance, food security
to conflict prevention, and so on. By investing in policy interventions to counter foreign malign
information manipulation that is targeted at USAID specifically (and that of our partners), USAID
will not only be able to continue its work; it will also be able to improve public perception of its
work, opening up new opportunities for collaboration with the people we hope to reach.
Opportunities and Risks of a Public Engagement:
Opportunities:
• This issue is going to get worse, and get more sophisticated. We should set up the next
administration to appreciate this problem, be persuaded to support continued work on it,
and finish building what we have identified as key gaps in our OKR recommendations,
most especially to USAID programs, partners, and people.
• Many of our peer development donor colleagues, bilateral and multilateral, are further
behind than USAID in getting organized and arriving at their convictions for how this
affects development, and how development assistance can be part of the response.
However, we have a big opportunity to prompt and then learn from our peer
development donor counterparts debates, and possibly shape a larger global
development response awareness and response effort.
• Making a public announcement on this issue (speech or op-ed) will also signal to our
Allies and adversaries how important it is to address this issue when iM/ FMI targets the
Allied development agenda - and it is the development agenda, that can make a
significant difference on the ground in shaping USAID partner countries for a better
future.

• One exception noting where a partner is far ahead of USAID is in the strategic
communications space, where the EU International Partnerships (EU/INTPA) that
manages development funding has a large flexible core budget at headquarters of
approximately $30 million specifically for communications campaigns, and has also set
aside significant budgets within their bilateral funding specifically for strategic
communications that dwarf what USAID has available for DOCs. EU/INTPA also
invested in regular country-level sentiment analysis so they can track trends, and track
narratives across media/social media. They are where we want to be if we can
overcome resource and capacity constraints.
Risks:
• A public speech so close to the end of this administration runs the risk of making
information manipulation/information integrity and resilience be perceived as a partisan
issue that is a priority for this administration and less welcome in the next. We are still
dealing with the 1st amendment misconceptions, and the GEC appears to be a victim of
that distrust.
• We believe the information manipulation issues should and probably will motivate a
national security coordination and response need in the next administration, but will a
public event or an oped by A/AID with a highly visible Biden administration official help or
hurt that compared to senior level handover conversations with the incoming team?
Frankly, a "mic drop" moment probably won't help our goal. It's laudable to go public and
call it out like our other USG exposures, and there is great value, but is it worth the
politicization risk when there already are House Judiciary Committee and private
litigation inquiries that have created a chilling effect on our staff?
• For the career staff who see the development damage information manipulation causes
to our U.S. taxpayer-funded activities and relationships, what's the best way to protect
that attention and nascent effort with a new team coming into USAID?

LAC/ DAA Mileydi Guilarte's Participation in a Meeting with Meta
April 9, 2024, 1:30-2:30pm
Ronald Reagan Building (RRB) Meeting Room LAC Large Conference Room (5.09.040)
Google Meet
Context:
Meta's Director of Executive Branch Public Policy, Sandra Luff, reached out to you and
LAC AA Marcela Escobari to request a meeting given that Íñigo Fernández, Meta's Public Policy
Director for Meta in Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean will be in Washington, D.C. this
week. Meta requested a meeting "to provide an overview of our key workstreams, including an
update on Meta initiatives in the region, how we are addressing the root cause of migration,
and election integrity." (Tab 1) This meeting follows several engagements that LAC Bureau staff
have had with Meta, and with Mr. Fernandez in particular, over the last three years. Per GC
guidance, this meeting should not discuss specific Meta content or posts. If the conversation
veers toward discussions about having specific posts or content removed, retained, posted, or
promoted, USAID should redirect the conversation. USAID will mainly be in listening mode and
use additional talking points to follow-up on information shared or questions posted by Meta.
(Complete GC guidance in Tab 2)
Desired outcomes
• Listen to Meta's presentation of key workstreams, updates on initiatives in the region,
how they are addressing the root causes of migration, and election integrity.
• Express appreciation for Meta and Mr. Fernandez' engagement with USAID's LAC Bureau
and work with Central America Missions, including on election integrity, and under the
interagency Voices initiative and Central America Forward (CAF).
Participant List and Run-of-Show
The meeting will be held in the Ronald Reagan Building (RRB) and will be conducted in
English. As Meta requested the meeting, you will open the meeting, provide brief remarks, and
then give them the floor to hear their remarks. In line with GC guidance, you will mainly be in
listening mode, provide broad responses and turn to staff attending as needed, without
committing to concrete actions or next steps. Vera Zakem will join the meeting in-person at
1:50pm ET due to previous meeting commitments. She may provide some remarks when she
joins.
Participants
Meta
• Íñigo Fernández Baptista, Director of Public Policy for Mexico, Central America,
and the Caribbean
• Brian Townsend, Public Policy Manager for South America
1

• Deborah Galindo, Public Policy Manager for Mexico, Central America & Caribbean
• Sandra Luff, Director of Executive Branch Public Policy
• Molly Montgomery, Director of Public Policy
USAID
• Mileydi Guilarte, LAC DAA
• Greg Howell, LAC SDAA
• Vera Zakem, Chief Digital Democracy and Rights Officer, DRG Bureau
• Martin McLaughlin, CAM Office Director
• Daniella Burgi-Palomino, DRG Specialist, LAC/RSD
• Cara Thanassi, DRG Specialist, LAC/RSD
• Chantal Agarwal, DRG Specialist, LAC/RSD
• Carrie Mitchell, DRG Team Lead, LAC/RSD
• Chris Cole, Deputy Director, LAC/RSD
• Chioma Ayogu, GC/DDE
• Alex Spevack, Economic Growth Offices, LAC/RSD
• Valeria Toledo, Program Analyst, LAC/FO
• Na-Yeon Park, Democracy Officer, LAC/CAM
Talking Points
Opening remarks
• Thank you, Sandy and Íñigo for reaching out and meeting with us.
• I understand Marcela already shared her transition news with you.
• With Marcela's departure, our colleague Michael Camilleri will serve as
Acting LAC Assistant Administrator as of next week. I think you may know
him from his time leading the Northern Triangle Taskforce.
• In my capacity as Deputy Assistant Administrator, I will continue to cover
Central America and Mexico.
• Let me just say at the outset that we have been very pleased to engage with
Meta over the last three years on issues related to Central America.
• I think the last time I saw you, Sandy, was in Denver, Colorado on the
sidelines of the Cities Summit in April last year.
• Íñigo, thank you for all your engagement under the interagency Voices
initiative, including your participation in events organized at previous
iterations of the Central America Donors Forum and at our side event at
2

RightsCon in Costa Rica last year. I know civil society organizations greatly
valued your remarks and willingness to engage in frank conversations.
• We've also appreciated your and Deborah's willingness to engage with our
Missions in the region on capacity-building opportunities for civil society
organizations, including around fact-checking, elections-related training in
Guatemala, as well as on training for our own communications staff.
• I know we shared some feedback with you on the Guatemala training held
last year. I'd be curious to hear about how you've adapted your training for
CSOs since then.
• Other areas that we hear CSOs and independent media need support on is
expanding their audience reach and countering information manipulation.
• We value your contributions towards the Vice President's Central America
Forward initiative to create economic opportunity in northern Central
America. Your commitment to train 250,000 youth, entrepreneurs and small
business owners in El Salvador, Guatemala, and Honduras by 2025 is
admirable.
• We look forward to hearing about your current work in the region and
specific issues you'd like to raise with us.
• I am joined by colleagues who cover democracy, rights, and governance,
elections, and economic growth issues for the region.
• I understand that my colleague Vera Zakem will join the meeting in a few
minutes.
Additional points to use only if needed to respond to Meta questions or for
information-sharing purposes
Voices initiative, civic space
• Since the launch of the interagency Voices initiative in 2022, we have
brought together civil society, donors, and the private sector together
around the three Voices pillars-Promoting digital democracy and countering
digital authoritarianism; promoting freedom of expression and
strengthening independent media; and countering criminalization and
providing protections for those who are targeted.
3

• ASK: The next Central America Donors Forum will be in October in
Antigua, Guatemala. Are you or your colleagues planning on
attending?
• We remain concerned about the trends of digital repression and targeted
attacks against civil society organizations, independent media outlets, and a
range of democracy and anti-corruption activists.
• ASK: Are you seeing similar trends in the region? How are you
engaging with civil society organizations and independent media to
address digital challenges?
• USAID is building the capacity of civil society organizations and independent
media to counter information manipulation and build resilience to digital
threats.
• ASK: Thanks for sharing about how you are engaging with civil society
organizations in the region. What new training and resources have
you developed to assist CSOs, independent media outlets and
journalists in these contexts, including any resources to expand their
audience reach?
Elections
• Thanks for sharing your work on elections in the region.
• We are monitoring the upcoming elections in the region closely, including
the Dominican Republic general elections on May 19th; Mexico's elections
on June 2nd, and Venezuela' elections on July 28th.
• ASK: With this year being the Year of Elections, how are you engaging
with civil society organizations and independent media in the region
around training and technical support so they are better equipped to
combat election-related information manipulation and foreign malign
influence?
• As USAID, we are closely tracking the elections in Mexico together with the
interagency. We continue our work with CSOs and independent media on
human rights, rule of law, transparency, and anti-corruption efforts. We are
concerned that violence against journalists usually increases in an election
year.
4

Central America Forward / Central America & Mexico Economic Growth
• Our Mission in Guatemala has been in conversations with the new
government in Guatemala around creating a network of micro, small, and
medium sized enterprise (MSME) innovation centers, especially as a way of
jump-starting growth in rural areas.
• USAID has worked with private sector partners in Guatemala to provide free
internet access in rural areas, with important knock-on effects on health,
education, and economic growth.
• ASK: Would there be interest in follow-up conversations to explore
ways for Meta to engage in these important initiatives?
• Are you familiar with USAID's eTrade Alliance? It is a Global Development
Alliance (GDA) between 13 leading private sector partners and USAID to
enable MSMEs to export using ecommerce.
• ASK: Would there be any interest in learning more about the eTrade
Alliance and how Meta could support activities?
• USAID is investing in the economic development of Mexico's southern
states and we participate with Ambassador Salazar in coordinating the USG
agencies and the American Chamber of Commerce.
• ASK: We would be happy to meet with Meta in Mexico to discuss how
we can cooperate and multiply the impact of our work in southern
Mexico.
Red Flags
If raised, harmful content moderation
• Meta-We have noticed a growing trend of inflammatory language posted on
our platforms. What does USAID think should be done about it?
• (Redirect) Thanks for raising this. Protecting civil society organizations
and human rights defenders is a priority for us. We appreciate your
attention to these issues and to your work with civil society
organizations around digital repression.
5

Background
Meta is the parent company of Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp. It also owns
CrowdTangle, a research and analysis tool that pulls in content and data from across Meta's
platforms.
According to the agency FAQs on Communications with Social Media Companies, on
October 5, 2023, State issued updated guidance (23 STATE 108554) regarding communications
with social media companies in light of the recent Fifth Circuit decision in Missouri v. Biden. As a
result of the decision, which significantly narrowed the injunction, USAID is no longer prohibited
from communicating with social media companies about content moderation in concert with
State (or other parties). Prior to the meeting, LAC/RSD/DRG staff reached out to the office of
the General Counsel (GC) to confirm our ability to take this meeting. General Counsel confirmed
that we were able to and provided some guardrails and recommendations for the conversation
from internal agency Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) on communications with social media
companies. If possible, USAID should stick to flagging general issues or trends or discussion of
what Meta and USAID are doing programmatically or via policy to address those issues or trends
and redirect or table anything that is potentially a landmine or complicated.
Different offices within USAID have interacted with Meta. For example, the Information,
Technology and Research Hub as well as the DRG Bureau-Global Technology Trends (GTT) have
met with Meta numerous times at a working level to discuss information integrity, resilience,
and digital democracy issues. Vera Zakem, USAID's Chief Digital Democracy and Rights Officer,
has also met with Meta for a variety of reasons corresponding to strengthening information
integrity and resilience during her tenure at USAID. She was on a panel with Iñigo Fernandez
Baptista, Director of Public Policy for Meta in Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean, at
Rights Con in 2023.
Engagement with Meta under the interagency Voices initiative
The CAM Office has engaged with Mr. Íñigo Fernández and Ms. Deborah Galindo on a
variety of occasions. In response to an invitation from the Northern Triangle Task Force, Mr.
Fernández participated as a panelist for a discussion under the interagency Voices initiative
focused on closing civic space at the 2022 Central America Donors Forum (CADF). At CADF, he
also engaged extensively with attendees. He was also invited to speak as a panelist on the
"Advancing Digital Democracy" Panel II of the joint USAID-State Department closed-door side
event at the RightsCon Summit in Costa Rica on June 5, 2023 "Voices: Promoting Digital
Democracy & Countering Digital Authoritarianism in Central America." Responding to calls from
partners for more regional and thematically focused discussions under the initiative, the event
brought together over 70 stakeholders from civil society organizations (CSO), independent
media, donors, the private sector, and implementing partners from the United States, Mexico,
Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, and Costa Rica. As a part of this effort, USAID also
supported close to thirty representatives from CSOs and independent media from Central
America to attend the RightsCon Summit.
LAC CAM Mission engagement with Meta (Comms, elections integrity, CSO trainings)
6

The LAC Bureau and Missions have engaged with Meta on various occasions over the last
two years. Under the directive of the LAC Bureau Tactical Plan, engagement in 2023 entailed
having Meta connect certain CSO partners with the International Fact Checking Network (IFCN)
so that they can have access to opportunities and resources to become IFCN-certified fact
checkers. Meta also offered a series of training sessions to CSOs on its community standards
and approach to combat information manipulation as well as tools to navigate its platforms. LAC
Comms also organized two sessions with Meta in September and October 2023 for over a dozen
Mission DOCs on Communications Digital Training and Speech and Integrity Training.
A full list of bilateral Mission engagements with Meta can be found in the Reference
documents. Engagements have included dialogues between Meta and CSOs and
awareness-raising, training and tools for building CSO resilience on information manipulation.
Mr. Fernandez and Deborah Galindo have been responsive to Mission requests for information
on Meta initiatives and training for CSOs in the Central America and Mexico region.
Prior to the Guatemalan elections, in March 2023, USAID LAC/DRG, DDI/DRG Center and
USAID Guatemala/ Post had a call with Meta's Public Policy Team for Mexico, Central America,
and the Caribbean to understand Meta's approach to the elections in Guatemala, share what
the USG is doing, and to identify possible areas for coordination and collaboration. Meta shared
information about their ongoing work in Guatemala ahead of the elections which includes
working with the electoral authority and political parties and providing them with training on
the best use of their platforms and Meta's transparency tools for ads, as well as partnering with
experts, civil society, and journalists to mitigate misinformation during the electoral process.
Meta offered Post/ Mission a version of their training for USG partners on ads transparency
tools; best use of Meta platforms; and community standards. The training was held on May 31st
in collaboration with the International Republican Institute (IRI). Feedback on the training was
shared with Meta by USAID LAC in June 2023. (See tab 3 for email exchange) There was no
further communication or update from Meta on how they incorporated the feedback into
future training. Additional areas identified by USAID Guatemala for Meta engagement include
addressing information manipulation, identifying and removing coyote and other scam
accounts, prevention and response to fraud, trafficking in persons (TIP), human smuggling/
irregular migration, and improving coordination and activism related to extortion, child
pornography, and online harassment.
LAC DAA Guilarte met with Sandra Luff and Catherine Eng of Meta at the Cities Summit
in Denver, Colorado in April 2023. According to the trip report (reference doc) they discussed
Meta's work on digital literacy, the interagency Voices initiative, and the broader relationship
with Meta.
While not directly with USAID, Meta is supporting the USG efforts to bring greater
development to Mexico's underdeveloped southern states. On August 30, 2023, Meta organized
"MetaDay", an event in Villahermosa, Tabasco which highlighted results of various digitization
initiatives, including the training of over 700 small businesses on the use of WhatsApp,
Instagram, Facebook and other Meta tools to find customers and increase sales. Meta's training
programs are in Spanish and in indigenous languages. This focus on accessibility allowed 300
members of indigenous communities in Mexico to benefit from their programs.
On elections, USAID Mexico has no specific elections programming. USAID does have
support for journalist protection, as violence against journalists has increased in past electoral
7

periods. USAID will support an NGO network that monitors, provides security-oriented training
for journalists, accompanies cases, and engages in advocacy. In Chiapas, USAID launched a
specific protocol on human rights defender protection in the elections, but the federal GOM
and other states are just relying on existing protection measures. USAID partner, the
International Center for Journalists, will train journalists to provide high-quality electoral
reporting in northern border states. USAID also partners with the National Protection
Mechanism and some state-level protection mechanisms to provide effective protection to
threatened journalists.While USAID/Mexico has no direct elections programming, it is closely
monitoring the electoral landscape and how political transitions will affect programming.
Activities will continue as planned in their implementation schedule. USAID is coordinating and
communicating closely with State DRL who is supporting some small efforts with IRI around the
elections.
Under the Citizens Empowered Activity (CEA) in El Salvador, Meta held a training for
CSOs in early 2023 entitled "Boost Your Cause." The U.S. Embassy and USAID attended Meta's
"Industry Day" in San Salvador in the fall 2023.
In Nicaragua, Meta's assistance has been strictly technical, case-by-case is where we've
seen the most engagement. Given sensitivities due to the restricted operating context, USAID
interactions have gone through the Digital Security IP who reaches out to Meta technical
contacts directly and reports back to USAID. The Mission contacted Meta for assistance with 13
emergency cases (affecting almost 1M audience members), and Meta helped recover some
accounts for a few key media outlets. For example, USAID's key media partner's FB account was
hacked by bitcoin ransomware and was down for two weeks. After the outlet was forced into
exile, Facebook is the primary channel for informing their audience of 300K Nicaraguans. Meta
helped recover it quickly.
Engagement with Meta under Central America Forward (CAF)/ PCA/ Economic Growth issues
On March 25, 2024, VPOTUS announced $1 billion in new private sector commitments,
including Meta's 3-year commitment to train250,000 youth, entrepreneurs and small business
owners in El Salvador, Guatemala, and Honduras by July 2025. Additionally, Meta is supporting
an initiative to help over 9,000 women from Guatemala, El Salvador, and Honduras including
women who lead small and medium-sized enterprises to establish their online presence, seize
the opportunities afforded by immersive technologies such as augmented reality, access
financial services, and expand their operations to international markets.
eTrade alliance ([link omitted] is an alliance of
private sector entities w/ USAID that works to facilitate cross border trade. Meta is committing
to work with SMEs in the context of CAF. An opportunity for Meta engagement is around
supporting SME innovation centers economically or with training. Meta's work in this space
entails getting people to transact on their platforms. Meta has also worked on expanding access
to the internet, in some cases offering people free access to Facebook.
