Belarusian independent media and BigTech, briefing paper, January 2024
Background
Country profile: digital Belarus, 2023. Key facts
•
Belarus is a country of 9.2M people
• 80% of the population leave in urban areas
54.0 percent of Belarus's population is female, while 46.0 percent of the population is male.
• There were 8.27million internet users in Belarus at the start of 2023, internet penetration
stood at 86.9 percent
• There were 4.27 million social media users in January 2023, equating to 44.9 percent of the
total population
• Atotal of 11.55 million cellular mobile connections were active in Belarus in early 2023, with
this figure equivalent to 121.3 percent of the total population
• Most popular OS include Android - 36.6%, Windows - 36.4% and iOS - 18.5%
• Google Search is the most popular search engine - 68.29%, tollowed by Yandex - 30.41%
• Google.com is the most popular website with 201.9M visits per month, of which 67% using
mobile phones
• Most popular Browsers in Belarus: Chrome 56.11%, Safari 20.8%, YandexBrowser -8.08%,
Opera 7.74%
• The state has designated most digital independent news resources as 'extremist' and blocked
access to them inside the county
• Largest independent media - Zerkalo, Nasha Niva, Euroradio, Belsat, etc - are registered
legal entities in the EU (Lithuania, Poland) (commercial and non-profit) due to mass
relocations in 2021-2022, but continue to produce content for the Belarusian audience (the
share of Belarusian audience across platforms is 50-70%). To reach their audiences, the
produce content for multiple platforms, use mirror and cloud services, the AMP project and
appeal to users to use VPN
• According to polls, in late 2023 circa 22% regularly consumed independent media and trust
them; 38.2% - disengaged audience, avoiding consuming news content. Before the blockings,
in 2020, independent media consumption was around 60%.
• Consumption of 'extremist' content is criminalised inside Belarus.
Current media context (January 2024)
State information policies and society
The actions oftheBelarusian authoritiesafterAugust 2020 in Belarus and the full scale invasion of
Ukraine unleashed by Russia have completely reshaped the Belarusian media market. The regime
pursues unrelenting and systemic repressions against the independent media, which include
prosecution of journalists, media managers and civil activists, their arrest, fines, searches of homes and
offices, expulsion from the country; internet censorship; labelling them as extremists. As of January
2024, 32 journalists are in prison, some were punished with harsh sentences of more than 10 years in
prison. Media consumption is also criminalised: a ban on the storage and distribution of 'extremist'
materials is enshrined in law; any public critical statements and comments are subject to administrative
and criminal penalties. The regime has effective control over traditional mass communication channels
- TV, radio, print media and has introduced heavy restrictions on the Internet.
Belarus authorities have aligned their manipulative narratives with Russia's, eroding national identity
and justifying Russia's aggression. Belarusian issues are integrated into the Russian context, portraying
Belarus as a subject within a federation. This copy-paste of Russian narratives aims to quell protest
sentiments, boost trust in Lukashenka, and legitimise Belarus's involvement in the war. The
independent media sector plays a crucial role in providing a truthful and propaganda-free perspective,
focusing on the Belarusian context amidst the challenges posed by the state propaganda and
disinformation and the increasing influence of the Russian information space.

Independent media ecosystem today
Ukraine, Germany, UK, Italy, Slovenia, Spain, Portugal, Latvia, and the U.S., with Poland and Lithuania
being popular legal bases within the EU. Many Belarusian media outlets are bilingual, with an increasing
focus on Belarusian-language or mixed content. Media hubs in Vilnius, Warsaw, Bialystok, Batumi, and
Ukraineserve as crucial support organisations, acting as secure resource centres, content production
hubs, and accelerators for new media projects.
The role of the Belarusian independent media
Despite operating outside Belarus, independent media remains crucial in preserving the nation's self-
consciousness, identity, and citizens' desire for independence amidst Russification efforts and
Lukashenka's anti-Belarusian policies. Serving as bridges to reality, independent Belarusian media help
the population navigate the trauma of the 2020 events. These media outlets act as influential points of
contact for democratic actors who cannot operate within Belarus, connecting with mass audiences
inside the country. Theeconomic sustainability of thesemedia projects relieson content quality,
audience trust, effective management, editorial potential, and donor support.
The impact of Belarusian independent media extends beyond information dissemination to shaping
public opinion, providing platforms for open discourse and diverse voices. In exile, these media outlets
contribute to transparency, acting as checks and balances crucial for a thriving democracy. Their
resilience in the face of challenges reflects a commitment to free speech and press freedom,
fundamental aspects of a democratic society. Thus, Belarusian independent media not only convey
information but also catalyse democratic
progress, fostering a society that values openness,
accountability, and active citizen participation.
Previous communication with BigTech
Belarus' independent media community and human rights community has been attempting to engage
in a dialogue with BigTech using various formats and at different platforms, including through assistance
of USAID, Access Now and within the RightsCon Conference. Most successful attempts have been
and Google, Apple, Cloudflare, Microsoft, some concrete use-case issues have been
resolved, but larger issues have not. Communication with other Big Tech companies, such as X, TikTok,
Telegram is absent.
Challenges related to BigTech
• Belarus's information sovereignty is under threat, Russian information influence inside
Belarus is increasing as non-politicised mass audiences increasingly consume Russian
narratives disseminated through Belarusian state information channels and Russian-produced
entertainment and learning/educational content. This also has a "crippling Russification
effect" on the Belarusian audience. Inter alia, this happens due to Belarus not being regarded
as a separate market.
Restricted availability of distribution channels by the independent media due to
restrictions by the Belarusian authorities. Information technology tools are playing an
increasing role in media production and distribution: content producers are heavily
dependent on BigTech (specifically, recommendation services of Meta, YouTube, Google
Search/News/Discover, TikTok, etc) for content distribution and are subject to targeted
technology-based repression and intervention by the Belarusian (and Russian) state. Potential
risks here also include further harsher restrictions on the Internet freedom in Belarus and her
likely integration with the "Russian Sovereign Internet".

Specific Issues flagged by the Belarusian media community (primarily concerning Google and
Meta, Microsoft)
1. Digital decolonisation (Google, Microsoft)
Belarus is a sovereign state heavily dependent on Russia. This dependence is amplified by Big Tech
company policies and business decisions. For instance, before 2022 Google's policies regarding
Belarus were decided by the Russian office and the Belarusian market was treated as a part of the
Russian segment of theInternet, based on the Russian language preferences of the majority of people.
With the start ofthe full-scale invasion and the closure of Googleoffice in Russia,there is no policy at
the company level towards Belarus.
Digital decolonisation in the case of Belarus has important cultural and social considerations. Poor
understanding of the context and non-existent policies towards Belarus only amplify Russian state
policies and speed up the process of Russification in Belarus.
There is a need for services to be tailored to the specific needs and cultural context of the Belarusian
society. Big Tech companies could customize their products and services to align with local language,
preferences, and user behaviours. We appeal to the Big Tech (Google in the first place) to foster
inclusivity and improve user experience, thereby providing the ability to cater to the unique requirements
Language localisation of the Belarusian segment as a separate one, which would include both
Russian (for Belarus) and Belarusian languages, could be a solution. This should lead to Big Tech
services being tailored for the Belarusian audiences seeking reliable and truthful information (ads of
Belarusian content for Belarusian users; targeting content for Belarusian audiences; etc.)
Having said that, we would like to refer to the case of Latvia, Estonia and Ukraine as inspiring case
studies/show cases, where a search in Russian provides information from local Russian-language
media. Also in the case of Belarus it is important to refrain from compliance with repressive state
regulations including content censorship, data localization and anti-extremism policies.
Belarusian content for Belarusian users
Localisation of Google services for Belarus (in Russian and in Belarusian) would fit in the
decolonisation trend, which is ongoing in the post-Soviet region (Ukraine, Georgia).
Google News and GoogleDiscover could consider the option to prioritize Belarusian news resources,
including in Belarusian, for those who search for news inside Belarus (current trend is that these
services offer a variety of Russian sources and only Belarusian state-controlled
sources for
Belarusians). That is, so that Belarusian media competed among each other, but not with the Russian
media. This could help fight the systemic dissemination of Russian manipulative narratives among
Belarusian audiences. (Examples of how Google services work for Belarus: [link omitted]

5..BY domain zone administration fully controlled by the state
In Belarus, the Operational and Analytical Center of the Presidential Administration (OAC), a security
agency, whose head is under the EU sanctions, is the administrator of the .BY domain zone (and the
less popular Cyrillic .бел). This agency is the successor of the Minsk Special Center of the State

Technical Commission of the USSR, changed its name several times and since the mid-90s received
the right to administer the.BY domain.
The OAC is directly involved in repressions in Belarus. In 2023, quoting formal grounds, the OAC started
taking away domain names from independent media. For instance, the OAC deprived the independent
publication EX-PRESS.BY of its domain name, requiring the owner, who fled from repression, to
personally appear at the OAC to confirm the domain registration data. Using a similar scheme, the
domain was taken away from BAJ and a number of other independent media.
In 2022, in Belarus, at the height of repression, the technical administrator of the.By domain zone
changed. Since 2010, it has been the "Reliable Programs" company (hoster.by), affiliated with the
TUT.by portal, the largest Belarusian media. In 2021, the portal was destroyed, the editorial staff was
partially arrested, and partially fled from Belarus.
The leaders of the Reliable Programs Unitary
Enterprise also went to prison. They were released, and a few months later transferred the right of
technical administration to Belarusian Cloud Technologies LLC, which is associated with the authorities.
We believe, the Internet governance procedure and ICANN procedures could be used to deprive the
OAC of the right to administer the.BY domain zone, since the OAC violates the main principle
underlying Internet governance - the balance of interests of civil society, authorities and business. In
Belarus,the governmentis illegitimate, and business,media,and civil society aresubject to targeted,
methodical repression.
Proposals and recommendations:
1) The key is the beginning of a dialogue between the Belarusian media community, representatives
of human rights organisations, researchers, international organizations and Big Tech with the
mediation of the European authorities in order to ensure that the Belarusian case - when technology
companies unintentionally pessimize quality resources blocked by the Belarusian authorities and
promote channels disseminating propaganda became the subject of discussion and development of a
strategy to solve this problem.
2) We propose to create a working group, comprised of representatives of DGConnect,
representatives of the Belarusian media sector, organizations involved in the development and
monitoring of journalistic standards, researchers and human rights activists, as well as
representatives of international organizations and BigTech to develop specific solutions: from the
possible labeling of channels affiliated with the state, as potentially harmful or spreading
disinformation, to helping to elaborating additional quality criteria for content in difficult and
uncontested environments. We are convinced that this work should be systematic, transparent and
regular. It cannot be reduced to negotiations between individual representatives of the Belarusian
media sector and representatives of BigTech, and the decisions should not depend on individual
personalities.
3) Ultimately, we are convinced that the Belarusian case is not unique, but perhaps one of the first in
a series of cases when technology becomes a tool for totalitarian and authoritarian regimes to put
pressure on civil society. And it requires a proper strategic approach, which is also taken into account
by European regulators.
4) We would like to emphasize that a cautious, human rights-centred approach when working with
Belarus should be implemented. Users already face draconian criminal charges for engagement on
social media or consumption of independent content delivered via social media and search engines,
while authoritarian regimes continue to spread propaganda and fear on those platforms. Big Tech
must recognise the role their products play and actively strive to mitigate the harm.

Potential issues that could also be discussed within the proposed working group and specific proposed
solutions:
• Develop due diligence plans and policies to prevent harmful overcompliance.
• Transparent policies and guidelines regarding content quality used by different BigTech
companies for content moderation.

sensitive profiles.

SENSITIVE BUT UNCLASSIFIED
Shannon Green, Assistant to the Administrator
Round Table on Belarusian independent media organizations' challenges with American tech
platforms
Friday, September 8, 2023, 13:30-14:00
NDI Office, 4 Islandijos str.
Context
You will have a 30-minute discussion with Belarusian independent media organizations
that are experiencing challenges using IT platforms developed and run by American tech
companies.
Desired Outcomes
That you have a greater understanding of the challenges that Belarusian independent
media organizations face disseminating their media products and creating sustainable business
models on IT platforms developed and run by American tech companies, so that you are better
positioned to advocate for them.
Participant List and Run-of-Show
This 30-minute meeting will be an in-depth update following USAID advocacy efforts on
behalf of Belarusian organizations to American big tech companies, especially Google and
Meta. These efforts have been led by Vera Zakem and Amy Malessa, Senior Digital Technology
Advisor, OTI. The round table discussion will include BCO's implementing partner supporting
independent media, Internews, and two of its local independent media partners: Press Club
Belarus, Zerkalo, and Nasha Niva. Translation will not be required.
• Introductions: Edgar will conduct a round of introductions. The allocated time for this
segment is 5 minutes.
• Internews, Press Club Belarus, and Zerkalo will brief you on their work that is affected by
American tech companies' policies regarding Belarus, how they have tried to address
these challenges, future strategies for addressing these challenges, and
recommendations on how they envision USAID advocacy could help them. The allocated
time for this segment is 20 minutes including your questions.
• Wrap-up session: Edgar will conclude the discussion. The allocated time for this segment
is 5 minutes.
Participants:
USAID:
Vera Zakem, Chief Digital Democracy and Rights Officer
Jenna Tajchman, Belarus Country Office Director
Edgar Mason, Belarus Country Office Deputy Director
Meewa Mull, Acting Country Representative, Belarus OTI
Mila Oleksiiuk, Democracy Specialist, USAID/Belarus
Marko Pjevic, Democracy Specialist, USAID/Belarus (on TDY from USAID/Serbia)

SENSITIVE BUT UNCLASSIFIED
Erin McCarthy, Senior Civil Society Advisor, USAID/E&E
Filip Jotevski, Special Assistant, USAID/DRG
Internews:
Greg Kehailia, The Media Activity CoP and Belarus Country Director
Yasia Karalevich-Kartel, Media Advisor
Press Club Belarus:
Natalia Belikova, Head of International Cooperation
Zerkalo (Zerkalo.io):
Aliaksandra Pushkina, Director
Nasha Niva:
Nastassia Rouda, Director
Talking Points
• USAID remains committed to assisting Belarusian organizations which work
to promote independent media and its role in a free, democratic Belarus.
This includes continuing to advocate on their behalf to American tech
companies.
• USAID recognizes that it is critical for Belarusian organizations and people
to have equitable access to these companies' services, platforms, and tools.
Without such access Belarusian organizations are significantly limited in
generating revenue, developing content, and reaching their desired
audiences. Such conditions make it extremely difficult to have sustainable
business models.
• USAID will continue to follow up with such companies as Meta and Google
regarding recognized inequities regarding Belarusians including the lack of
Belarusian as an official language on platforms for the purposes of searches
and monetization and not restricting access to exiled Belarusian
organizations' websites and content.
• For example, Vera has been communicating with Meta's European Policy
Team about the future of political ads in Europe given their challenges
related to compliance with the Digital Service Act.

SENSITIVE BUT UNCLASSIFIED
• What do you think should be the priorities for USAID advocacy efforts to
American tech companies on behalf of Belarusian organizations, including
independent media?
• In the digital space, what other areas do you think USAID could focus its
efforts to support Belarusian independent media that it hasn't yet been
working on?
• How have you been able to overcome the limitations and restrictions that
impede your ability to reach audiences through digital media?
• What do you see as likely future restrictions or trends that could make your
ability to function in the digital space more challenging?
Red Flags
• N/A
Background
Belarus challenges with Big Tech platforms
In response to an increase in recent concerns, in January USAID/Belarus brought out OTl's Senior Digital
Technology Advisor to meet with Belarusian democratic actors and identify the challenges that they are
having with U.S.-based technology companies, including Google (e.g. Search, YouTube), Meta (e.g.
Facebook, Instagram) and Twitter.
The following insights and recommendations are based on interviews with eleven Belarusian
organizations over the course of one week (January 23-27, 2023) in Poland and Lithuania, as well as
follow-up conversations. These organizations included major media organizations, leading outlets,
political actors, and activist content creators.
Most organizations have officially appealed these challenges directly to platforms with mixed results,
depending on their relationships with platform staff. There are early efforts by OST, the Press Council,
International Media Support, Internews and Access Now to advocate more effectively on behalf of all
Belarusian partners, including independent media organizations and civil society organizations. USAID
can and should complement those international efforts.
Thankfully, as a silver lining, there is no evidence that platforms are using official designations by the
Government of Belarus (e.g. the labeling of organizations as terrorist or extremist organizations) to
inform their account or content decisions to date.

SENSITIVE BUT UNCLASSIFIED
Here are the four main challenges and potential responses by USAID:
1. Organizations are having their content removed and pages restricted due to violations of
Meta's Terms of Service (a.k.a. "Community Standards")
Organizations are receiving notifications from Facebook and Instagram that their content violates
Meta's Terms of Service related to violence, graphic content, hate speech, and adult nudity. These
notifications vary in terms of their level of specificity - some link to the post (if it's flagged by a human
moderator), most do not (if it's flagged by a platform algorithm) - but none describe the violation in
sufficient detail to either fix the violation or prevent future violations.
There are a few contributing factors to this challenge. Terms of Service are broadly defined and enforced
mostly by platform algorithms that misinterpret slang and cultural context. Additionally, the algorithms
are not subject to public oversight and change frequently without prior notice. It is also unclear how
many human content moderators speak Belarusian and where they are located right now.
Why do Terms of Service violations matter? Three notifications result in restrictions against the
offending page, including a significant drop in organic distribution or reach (e.g. from 3 million to 100K in
one month). Additional notifications put the page at risk of being shut down and losing their entire
audience on the platform.
As a result of these violations, organizations are being more cautious in terms of what and how they
publish content. For example, partners are choosing to do softer content over hardcore news and
publishing less informal or live content which are popular formats.
Organizations are utilizing the official appeal process to appeal these violations with mixed results,
depending on their relationships with platform staff. This is a recurrent and labor intensive challenge -
successfully resolving one appeal after days or weeks of back-and-forth communication does not make
the account immune from future violations.
Potential Response by USAID: USAID/DC can elevate specific cases that have exhausted the official
appeal process (e.g. BelSat) back to Meta for further review. Meanwhile, USAID/Belarus can work with
the Press Council and Internews, one of Meta's Trusted Partners, to get their "inclusion list" of
independent media outlets (originally developed for "Ads for News") admitted to Meta's Cross Check
Program (a new program that vets media outlets, so they are no longer flagged for violations). The
"inclusion list" will need to be maintained across USAID/Belarus IPs and can be discussed at the
upcoming partners meeting. Once the "inclusion list" is updated and ready to go, USAID/DC can share it
with Meta.
2. Inability to promote content in Belarusian language across YouTube, Google Search, Discovery
and News, and the suspected down-ranking of content

SENSITIVE BUT UNCLASSIFIED
Organizations cannot promote or run small dollar ads on content in Belarusian language on Google
Display Network, most notably Google Search and YouTube. If accounts are caught trying to promote
content in Belarusian language, the user receives an "unsupported language" notification and their ad
campaign is turned off. It is unclear if the overall account is penalized.
In addition to content blocked for "unsupported language"
", content is also being blocked by Google
Display Network for covering "sensitive events". Most appeals related to "sensitive events" are
successfully resolved in favor of the user, but only after 1-3 days of back-and-forth communication when
the content is no longer relevant.
There is speculation that Google Search and YouTube recommendation algorithms are down-ranking
content in Belarusian language. It is unclear if that is true and Google staff deny it. The methods used by
partners to get content inside Belarus (e.g. website mirrors, external referral links from social media)
and their lack of knowledge about search engine optimization can also contribute to the down-ranking
of content.
Potential Response by USAID: USAID/DC was notified by OST on February 2 that Google added
Belarusian language to their product development calendar for the second half of 2023. This point
should be highlighted in future meetings between USAID/DC and Google leadership so that momentum
is not lost.
USAID/DC can also ask Google to speed up the appeal process for "sensitive events" from days to hours.
USAID/DC can ask Google and Jigsaw about technical options under development to deliver content to
citizens living under repressive regimes and encourage partnership with local organizations working
outside of Belarus.
Beyond working directly with Google, USAID/Belarus can fund research and development by local
emerging technology groups (e.g. Press Council's TechHub) to test and scale alternative content delivery
methods that do not down-rank content. USAID/Belarus can also fund independent consultants or
commercial digital agencies on retainer to improve partners' knowledge of search engine optimization
and how to optimize content for discovery across platforms.
3. The verification requirements in order to pay for and geographically target ads for social or
political content on Facebook and Instagram
Meta has a global policy related to the promotion of social and political content (again, broadly defined)
in an attempt to limit foreign influence or interference in domestic affairs. The ability to place small
dollar ads for social and political content requires page owners to submit a national ID card and use a
domestic bank for payment. In addition, the pages that pay for these ads are added to Facebook's public
Ad Library for seven years.

SENSITIVE BUT UNCLASSIFIED
At a meeting organized by the Press Council between partners and a Meta representative in November
2022, many organizations were surprised to learn about the existence of the Ad Library. There is
growing concern that the Government of Belarus will use the information already on Facebook's Ad
Library to detain, torture and persecute page owners or other active users associated with the page.
Right now, organizations are not providing this additional layer of verification and not marking their ads
as social or political on Facebook or Instagram for security reasons. If accounts are caught trying to
promote social or political content without properly labeling it, the user receives a notification and their
ad campaign is turned off. It is unclear if the overall account is penalized.
Potential Response by USAID: Given the security concerns of our partners, USAID/DC could ask Meta to
waive the verification requirement for social and political content targeted inside Belarus or remove
Belarusian organizations who are at-risk from the Ad Library. This response is politically sensitive since
Congress pushed for the creation of the Ad Library to increase public ad transparency and limit foreign
interference in U.S. domestic affairs after the 2016 election.
4. Growing concerns related to coordinated inauthentic behavior (e.g. bot networks, troll farms)
across all platforms
At this time, most of the views, reach and engagement with pro-Regime channels and pages that's
driving them up in search results (e.g. trending content) is believed to be organic traffic from human
users generated in-country or in the region. But, there's growing concern that state-affiliated actors are
using automated means to flood pages / channels and account owners with unfounded complaints,
including copyright violations and targeted threats.
There is a strong desire by multiple organizations to have a mechanism for flagging channels that spread
"propaganda", so they can be reviewed by platforms against their Terms of Service. Initial attempts to
do this have been ad hoc and with limited supporting evidence (e.g. individual anecdotes). There are
very few public reports on coordinated inauthentic behavior in and around Belarus that can be shared
with platforms right now.
Potential Response by USAID: USAID/Belarus can fund and elevate independent research and analysis
(e.g. iSANS, Stop Propaganda, MedialQ, Digital Skills Coalition Initiative) that demonstrates the origin,
methods and impacts of coordinated inauthentic behavior in the context of Belarus. USAID/Belarus can
also refer local partners into training programs (e.g. Digital Forensic Research Lab's Digital Sherlocks) to
build their capacity related to digital forensics and open source investigations.
Once USAID/DC has access to more credible reporting on coordinated inauthentic behavior, we can ask
platforms to review those reports and the related accounts against their Terms of Service. However,
USAID cannot ask for specific content or account takedowns. According to U.S. Government policy,
USAID can share independent research and analysis, but not dictate the specific course of action.

USAID Activity: The Media Activity in Belarus (TMA)

The Media Activity increases the supply of quality, socially relevant content and increases
citizens' demand for accurate, objective information. The Activity supports the production of
news, discussions, and infotainment. The activity also strengthens and expands the existing
media literacy activities, working with both media practitioners and citizens, exploring new
approaches like formal training for educators and civil society activists; integration of critical
thinking skills into school subjects. The deficit of empirical data and scientific research on this
topic in the country and the ability to implement iterative, adaptive approaches to assistance
further intensify the challenges in this area. To this end, the Activity aims to enhance local
research-based methodologies to inform advancing the integrity of the media space in Belarus.
Gregory Kehailia is the country director of Internews for Belarus and Chief
of Party of the USAID-funded TMA program. He is a political scientist and
has worked for two decades and half analyzing political processes and
implementing democracy, rights and governance programs in Southeast
Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa, and Middle East & North Africa. Previously, Greg
spent four years representing Internews in the Philippines, with a portfolio
focused on tackling disinformation and foreign influence operations and on protecting media
freedom and safety. Before the Philippines, Greg worked in Myanmar for over four years as
country director of The Carter Center, concentrating on electoral reform and observation as
well as on the Myanmar peace process, and as senior program manager of the
intergovernmental institution International IDEA, working embedded in the Myanmar's election
commission on the 2015 general elections. Formerly, Greg had worked in Washington DC at the
headquarters of IFES and IREX, in DR Congo as IFES country director, in Jordan and Iraq for the
United Nations, and in Egypt for the intergovernmental institution Anna Lindh Euro-
Mediterranean Foundation for Dialogue between Cultures. Following some years working for
grassroots civil society organizations in France, Greg had started his international career as a
diplomat of the European Union at the EU Embassies in Syria and Algeria, covering human
rights, democratization, violent extremism and forced disappearances. He is based in Vilnius.
Yanina Karalevich-Kartel has 10 years of experience as a journalist, editor,
media manager, and journalism trainer. Since 2022 she works as Media
Adviser in Internews Network. Before that she was the co-editor-in-chief of
CityDog.by, an online Minsk city magazine that is one of the country's most
innovative and high-quality outlets, where she started as a journalist and
executive editor in 2012. She is also the creator and editor of the
multimedia project 90s.by, which explores the transitional period of the
1990s in Belarus through photos, text, and historical artifacts. She holds a

Sciences at Belarusian State University.
Press Club Belarus' mission is to foster Belarusian independent media community development
in exile. Press Club Belarus' scope of activities includes: community and resilience building for
the Belarusian independent media sector; media-related training and education; media
intelligence and tech services and support for the community.
Natalia Belikova is the Head of International Cooperation of Press Club
Belarus, an umbrella organization for Belarusian independent media
outlets, which works to preserve Belarusian journalism and foster media
development in Belarus. Natalia, a trained international lawyer, has over 15
years of progressive professional experience in media development,
including within UN and OSCE systems. Her professional interests include
strategic communications, counteracting disinformation, media literacy,
strategic media development and analysis.
"Zerkalo" is one of the leading Belarusian independent media. The mission of the Zerkalo portal
is to give every user the opportunity to get objective information on his or her interests, expand
his or her horizons, and live life to the fullest. For almost two years now, the media has been
working in exile. All zerkalo.io content is published on the portal and in iOS and Android apps,
social networks, and messengers. "Zerkalo" audience on the portal has more than 2.5 million
unique users. The news published on the portal are viewed more than 30 million times a
month, and videos published on "Zerkalo" video platforms are viewed more than 60 million
times a month. Their total number of subscribers in social networks exceeds 2 million.
Aliaksandra Pushkina is director of Zerkalo. She is one of the team
members of former outlet "TUT.BY" who reactivated the largest
independent media outlet in Belarus in a new project "Zerkalo". She
specializes in communication strategy, PR, fundraising, and development of
related products or services. Ms. Pushkina has experience as the PR
manager of TUT.BY, Program director of the conference "Business Internet",
Brand-manager of Alfa-Bank Belarus, and Press-secretary of the national
women's basketball team of Belarus.

Nasha Niva is one of the oldest Belarusian socio-political publications, with more than 115
years of history. Today, Nasha Niva operates entirely online and is the second-most popular
online portal in the country and the first among Belarusian-speaking ones. Nasha Niva is a
nationally oriented media where the Belarusian language, culture, history, and independence
are key values. Nearly all independent media outlets have staff in prison in Belarus. Nasha
Niva's former chief editor Jahor Martynovich, released from prison on August 18, 2023 after

Nastassia Rouda has been working at Nasha Niva for over seven years. At
various times, she was a reporter, editor, deputy chief editor, and head of

the director of Nasha Niva and the host of the interview project on the TOK
YouTube channel. Previously, for four years, she worked as a journalist and
editor for the regional independent publication Rehiyanalnaja Hazeta.
